name: Junko Tabei
tagline: The woman who climbed above a world that told her to stay down
story:
In 1970s Japan, women were expected to pour tea, not climb mountains. When Junko Tabei founded the Ladies Climbing Club in 1969, male climbers mocked them. Sponsors refused funding. Society told her that mountains were no place for a woman, let alone a mother. She ignored all of it and set her sights on the highest point on Earth.

On May 4, 1975, at 12,500 feet on Everest's Lhotse Face, an avalanche buried Tabei and her team under a wall of snow and ice. She lost consciousness. When Sherpas dug her out, she could barely stand — her legs were battered, her body broken. Any reasonable person would have turned back. Tabei looked up at the summit and kept climbing.

Eleven days later, on May 16, 1975, Junko Tabei stood on top of the world — the first woman to ever summit Mount Everest. She was 35 years old, 4'9", and weighed barely 100 pounds. When reporters asked how it felt, she said simply: 'I can't understand why men make all this fuss about Everest. It's only a mountain.'

Tabei didn't stop there. She went on to become the first woman to complete the Seven Summits — the highest peak on every continent. Even after being diagnosed with cancer in 2012, she continued climbing. She summited her final peak from a wheelchair-accessible base camp, proving until her last breath that the size of your fight matters infinitely more than the size of your body.
